title: Monica's Saturday fast
hookLine: veils, kneeling, silence or sung responses: customs differ from parish to parish
tomorrow: Two forms of the Latin rite

lines: A VEIL IN A COAT POCKET.
cards: A lace veil, folded small, lives in the coat pocket of a woman who travels for work. One Sunday, in one city, she puts it on, and so do several women around her.
The next Sunday, in another city, she's the only one, and she wonders whether to take it off. In the first church the people kneel after the Lamb of God; in the second they stand until communion.
One choir chants the responses in Latin; across town, a guitar leads them in English. One parish keeps a long silence after communion; another goes straight to the announcements. Same Mass.
Same creed. Is somebody doing it wrong?

teach.b: Saint Augustine tells an old version in one of his letters. His mother, Monica, had moved to Milan, and she was troubled: back home she had fasted on Saturdays, and in Milan the church didn't.
Augustine asked the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. His answer, as Augustine reports it: when I'm here, I don't fast on Saturday; when I'm in Rome, I do.

teach.h: AMBROSE: FOLLOW THE CHURCH YOU'RE IN.
teach.b: Follow the custom of the church you're in. Augustine says he took that answer as if it had come from heaven.

Paul, writing to the Romans, who were arguing about food and holy days, he says in the Douay-Rheims: "One judgeth between day and day: and another judgeth every day: let every man abound in his own sense."
Then he tells them to stop judging each other.
The Church draws a line between what is shared and what is local. The faith, the sacraments, the heart of the Mass: these are one.
The Second Vatican Council said the Church doesn't want a rigid sameness in matters that don't touch the faith or the good of the whole community.

The instructions for Mass let each country's bishops adapt postures, and leave room for music, language and local devotion. So a veil worn by choice, a kneel or a stand, a chant or a hymn, can differ and both be faithful.

teach.h: LET EVERY MAN ABOUND IN HIS OWN SENSE.
teach.b: And customs carry love: a grandmother's mantilla, a parish's long silence. The question isn't whose custom wins. It's whether you can kneel beside someone else's.

how: Catholic customs at Mass vary by country and parish: some women wear a chapel veil and others don't, bishops' conferences adapt when the people kneel or stand, and parishes differ in music, language and silence. Visitors are generally expected to follow the custom of the parish they're in.

o: one faith and Mass, kept with different local habits
the rule that every parish must worship alike
old habits the Church asks people to set aside

games.q: who said what about customs — tap the pairs.
p: unsure whether to fast on Saturday
asked the bishop, and told the story
let every man abound in his own sense

s: Ambrose fasted on Saturday in Rome but not in Milan
that's his answer as Augustine reports it: follow the custom of the church you're in.
the Church wants every parish to do every part of Mass exactly alike
the Second Vatican Council said it doesn't want rigid sameness in matters that don't touch the faith.
where people kneel or stand at Mass is decided by each bishops' conference
the instructions for Mass let bishops' conferences adapt postures for their countries.

games.q: you're Monica. you've moved to Milan, and the church here doesn't fast on Saturday the way your home church did. what do you do?
o: keep your old fast, so no one thinks you've gone soft.
have your son ask the bishop, Ambrose, what to do.
stop going to church until you find one that does it your way.
games.why: Augustine asked Ambrose for her. the bishop said he fasted on Saturday in Rome and not in Milan: follow the church you're in. Augustine says he took it as if from heaven.

practice: Bring to mind a church habit that isn't yours, a veil, a raised hand, and one real person who keeps it. Ask what it might hold for them: a memory, a family, a way of saying yes to God.
If you pray, pray for that person by name; if you don't, wish them well in the thing they love.

wordCard.voice: Many customs. The Catholic understanding that one faith and one Mass can be kept with different local habits: veils, postures, music and silence. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, custom: the word Church law uses for a long-kept local practice.

carryVoice: Your line: one faith, many local customs. One faith can kneel in more than one way. Go gently.

sources.q: One judgeth between day and day: and another judgeth every day: let every man abound in his own sense.
